title: Provider Enforces Undocumented Route Limit
symptom: One office loses connectivity to a public service endpoint; its only path used one BGP session that was torn down. Likely cause: The upstream provider had a hidden limit on routes accepted from us, and normal growth crossed it.
checks: Check session state and any max-prefix or teardown reason on both sides.
Ask the provider what limit they enforce.
resolution: Have the provider raise the limit substantially.
Verify: Session re-establishes and the office reaches the endpoint.
Afterwards: Add a second, independent internet path from a different provider.
Afterwards: Get provider-side limits documented.

title: Provider Maintains Both Redundant Circuits At Once
symptom: A facility loses nearly all outbound paths for several hours. Most of its routes are normally advertised from another site. Likely cause: The two circuits between the sites were the two the provider serviced at the same time.
checks: Check provider maintenance notices for every circuit between the two sites.
resolution: Nothing to fix; the outage ends when maintenance finishes and both circuits return.
Verify: Both circuits are up and routes are advertised again.
Afterwards: Watch for overlapping maintenance windows on redundant circuits.
Afterwards: Document a manual backup path.

title: Stuck Input Buffer Drops Multicast On One Port
symptom: Multicast through one specific port is dropped, causing a monitoring outage for a downstream system. Discards climb steadily. Likely cause: A stuck internal buffer, a known issue with that hardware model.
checks: Check discard counters on the port and the vendor's known-issue list for that model.
resolution: Shut down the affected interface to stop the loss.
Verify: Monitoring recovers and discards stop.
Afterwards: Upgrade firmware on the surrounding hardware as the permanent fix.
Afterwards: Match symptoms against vendor bug lists early.

title: Retiring Old Routers Pulls Routes From The New Ones
symptom: About 10 minutes of lost connectivity to an outside office and several broadcast channels while shutting down a temporary bridge between old and new routers. Likely cause: The new routers still relied on the old ones to advertise certain routes to the provider.
checks: Check whether a bridge or old device was just shut down or removed, and which routes it advertised.
resolution: Revert the change immediately.
Verify: The path to the outside office and channels is restored.
Afterwards: Before decommissioning, map everything still leaning on the old gear, not just its original role.
Afterwards: Let the new routers advertise their routes independently first.

title: Replacement Switch Auto-Loads A Stale Configuration
symptom: Object storage behind content delivery loses connectivity during a hardware swap for a memory fault. Likely cause: The replacement switch auto-loaded a leftover, incompatible configuration, breaking the switch pairing it needed.
checks: Check what configuration the new switch actually loaded at setup.
resolution: Take over configuration directly, restore the correct ports, and shift traffic to unaffected sites.
Recovery took about 1.5 hours.
Verify: Storage access is confirmed clean.
Afterwards: Require a clean, verified starting configuration before any replacement switch connects to the live network.

title: Mismatched Link Bundle After A Router Swap
symptom: A national sports feed returns playback errors shortly after an edge router is swapped to another vendor's hardware. Likely cause: The new router's multi-link bundle to a downstream appliance was configured slightly differently from what the other end expected.
checks: Check bundle (link aggregation) settings on both ends of every link to the downstream appliance.
resolution: Correct the configuration.
Playback returned about 25 minutes after the first report.
Verify: The logical connection is up and playback is clean.
Afterwards: Run a post-change check of every downstream dependency before closing a hardware swap.

title: Multicast Joins Ignored After A Hardware Migration
symptom: Broadcast receivers lose multicast subscriptions after moving to new network hardware. Likely cause: A required setting enabling multicast routing was not applied on one interface, so join requests were never answered.
checks: Check that multicast routing is enabled on every interface involved in the migration.
resolution: Apply the missing setting.
No rollback was needed.
Verify: Test a device joining from multiple locations.
Afterwards: Review routing protocols as carefully as cabling in a migration.
Afterwards: Keep an open item with the vendor to confirm no similar surprises.

title: Resync Wipes Settings Applied Outside The Management Platform
symptom: Monitoring for a whole site goes dark and virtualization hosts falsely appear offline after a resync on the management platform. Likely cause: Interface configurations applied directly on the command line were unknown to the platform and were erased.
checks: Check interface configs on the affected switches against the last backup.
resolution: Restore the lost interface configurations from the separate network backup system.
Verify: Monitoring returns once the configs are reapplied.
Afterwards: Make every change through the tool, with no side doors.
Afterwards: Update standard templates so no unmanaged workaround is needed.

title: Duplicate Loopback Addresses On New Leaf Switches
symptom: Signal is lost across a set of broadcast feeds from one facility during live events. Likely cause: Two new leaf switches had a loopback address already used by existing switches.
checks: Check loopback addresses on newly deployed switches against existing ones.
resolution: Shut down the conflicting uplinks and reassign the new switches.
Verify: Feeds are restored.
Afterwards: Keep the address-in-use check as a standing step for new hardware.

title: Pairing Feature Enabled On Switches With No Partner
symptom: After maintenance, new hosts on a virtual network segment reach each other but nothing outside it. Likely cause: Two leaf switches had switch pairing enabled with no actual partner, leaving an internal control interface down and breaking the tunneling.
checks: Check whether pairing is configured on switches that have no partner, and the state of the control interface.
resolution: Remove the leftover pairing configuration and bring the control interface up.
Verify: Hosts reach destinations outside the segment.
Afterwards: Confirm a switch is configured the way a new feature expects before go-live.

title: Fiber Cut Causes Asymmetric Routing And A Second Regional Outage
symptom: After a fiber cut, failover did not behave as designed. Traffic left by one path and returned by another, and security devices dropped it. An emergency single-path fix then broke two other regions. Likely cause: Asymmetric routing through stateful security devices. The two other regions were missing route announcements needed for the forced path.
checks: Compare outbound and return paths for affected flows.
List which regions lose routes under the forced path.
resolution: Force traffic through the single healthy path, then check every region that change touches.
Revert once the fiber is repaired.
Verify: Flows are symmetric and no other region lost reachability.
Afterwards: Add the missing route announcements.
Afterwards: Remove temporary workarounds rather than living with them.

title: Out-Of-Process Routing Edit Leaks A More Specific Route
symptom: A publishing platform loses connectivity during a cloud networking migration, and a bad route appears from a legacy environment. Likely cause: An engineer troubleshooting something else edited routing outside the change process, leaking a more specific route that wins over the general one.
checks: Check recent routing edits on the legacy environment, and which specific prefix is being advertised.
resolution: Revert the edit.
The route disappeared about 20 minutes after the ticket opened.
Verify: The offending prefix is gone from the table and the platform is reachable.
Afterwards: Route in-flight troubleshooting changes through approval before they touch anything live.

title: Maintenance On The Last Surviving Undersea Path
symptom: Two continents lose connectivity entirely. Likely cause: The primary undersea link was already down awaiting a repair ship, and planned maintenance took out the only remaining path.
checks: Check the status of every path between the sites, including long-running repairs, and any maintenance scheduled on the survivor.
resolution: The vendor tried remote restoration without success.
An on-site power cycle of a piece of equipment brought connectivity back.
Verify: Both sites are reachable over the restored path.
Afterwards: Check for other planned maintenance before scheduling your own.
Afterwards: Do not let a temporary single point of failure become permanent.

title: Redistribution Conflict Stops A Data Center Advertising Itself
symptom: A data center loses internet and cloud connectivity and several streaming platforms show error spikes. The change looked fine right after being applied. Likely cause: A policy change to match a new internal standard conflicted with static route redistribution, so the site stopped announcing its own address space.
checks: Check whether the site's prefixes are still being advertised upstream, a few minutes after any policy change.
resolution: Revert both routers to the previous configuration.
Recovery followed in about 10 minutes.
Verify: Prefixes are visible externally again and error rates are back to normal.
Afterwards: Wait for the change's real effect before closing the post-change check.
Afterwards: Classify this kind of change as higher risk.

title: A And B Feeds Share A Hidden Dependency
symptom: Several live events lose picture, fully or partly, with gaps in the recorded archives. Likely cause: One facility's maintenance took the A path to both destination data centers. Both sites then reconnected through the same shared recovery path, flooding and degrading the B feed.
checks: Check whether A and B share an originating facility or a recovery path.
resolution: Mitigate the shared recovery path.
Feeds stabilized about 1 hour 20 minutes after mitigation began.
Verify: Both feeds are clean and archives are recording.
Afterwards: Send A and B to entirely separate destinations.
Afterwards: Review the whole path end to end for shared dependencies.

title: Cleanup Removes Links A Precision Timing Protocol Needs
symptom: Playback problems appear across live streaming platforms, with timing alerts, after a network cleanup. Likely cause: Links thought redundant were needed for precision timing traffic, and the remaining paths could not carry it the same way.
checks: Check whether the removed links carried timing traffic, and compare the timing alerts' start time against the change.
resolution: Revert the cleanup.
This was done within about 1 hour of the first alerts.
Verify: Timing alerts clear.
Afterwards: Preserve enough dedicated paths for timing traffic before any further cleanup.

title: Load Balancer Service Engines Crash Repeatedly
symptom: Service engines crash repeatedly over about a week, isolated to one newly created group. Likely cause: A known vendor bug tied to memory reserved for debug and trace logging. The new group had missed a safeguard the rest of the fleet had.
checks: Check whether the failing group matches the settings of the stable fleet, and the debug-logging memory reservation.
resolution: Turn the debug and trace memory setting down to the minimum.
The group stayed stable for well over a day.
Verify: No crashes occur and the vendor case is closed.
Afterwards: Plan the software upgrade the vendor recommended.
Afterwards: Check that new groups inherit lessons learned by older ones.

title: Circuit Change Takes A Few Hundred Live Channels Off The Air
symptom: Publishing for a few hundred live channels stops for about 20 minutes after routine circuit maintenance at one data center. Likely cause: The change landed on infrastructure that had quietly become load-bearing for many channels.
checks: Check what rides on the circuit before you change it.
resolution: Revert as soon as the impact is clear.
Channels returned almost immediately.
Verify: Channel publishing counts are back to normal.
Afterwards: Move the busiest channels to a healthier data center.
Afterwards: Treat small changes to shared circuits as high impact.

title: BGP Sessions Drop Silently On A Legacy Router With A Known Firmware Bug
symptom: A legacy data center router drops its BGP sessions to the cloud with no log cause. Several unrelated tools and teams page at once. Likely cause: A known vendor bug in old firmware, fixed in a newer release never installed because the site was being retired. Legacy tools and a login service all routed through that one router.
checks: Check the firmware version against vendor known-bug lists, and which tools and services depend on this router for cloud access.
resolution: Open a case with the vendor and recover the sessions.
Treat the simultaneous pages as one incident.
Verify: Sessions are up and the dependent tools, including deployments and login, work again.
Afterwards: Patch or isolate hardware even when it is slated for retirement.
Afterwards: Map what leans on a single legacy path.
